title: Set up a belief, then knock it down
subtitle: Text Structure and Purpose · 19 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **19 of the official questions in Text Structure and Purpose are this one** — 3 Easy, 5 Medium, 11 Hard.
It is top-heavy: most versions are Hard, so it only earns study time once your target actually requires that tier.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- The text starts with what 'many researchers assume,' 'people long thought,' or 'some studies suggest.' It then offers a finding or example that complicates that view.
- The question may ask about structure or main purpose.
- Correct choices use words like 'challenges,' 'complicates,' or 'cautions against overstating.'

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Find the belief at the start and decide whether the author endorses or doubts it, using signals like 'however,' 'but,' 'we should not overstate,' or 'busted the myth.' 2) Treat the rest of the text as evidence for that doubt.
- 3) Pick the choice whose verb says 'questions' or 'challenges' and names the right belief, not the evidence.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: Most of the text is about the study or example, so you pick 'to describe an experiment' or 'to present findings about X.' That is what the text contains, not what it is for.
On the harder items, the other trap is a choice that claims the author rejects the idea entirely when the text only warns against overstating it.

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
Most of the text is about the study or example, so you pick 'to describe an experiment' or 'to present findings about X.' That is what the text contains, not what it is for.
On the harder items, the other trap is a choice that claims the author rejects the idea entirely when the text only warns against overstating it.
